metadata.title: Meta Pauses Zuckerberg Share Plan During Investor Legal Fight

content.text:
(Bloomberg) -- Meta Platforms Inc. said it will hold off on distributing a new class of shares while a legal fight plays out with investors who oppose the tech giant's plan to fund the company's artificial intelligence investments without diluting Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg's stake.

The plan called for Meta to create a new category of non-voting Class C shares on Jan. 19 that would be issued later as a dividend to existing investors, including Zuckerberg. The arrangement would also allow Zuckerberg, Meta's co-founder and the world's fifth-richest person, to sell some of that stock without reducing his majority voting power.
In a court filing Wednesday, Meta agreed to hold off issuing any Class C shares during the legal fight, which is set for trial in Delaware Chancery Court in April.
"In the best interest of our shareholders, we are seeking a final determination as quickly as the court will allow, and we will vigorously defend against these claims," Meta said in a statement.
The company has said the new share class is critical to helping it raise capital needed to build out AI infrastructure to compete in the race to dominate that field, and that it must move quickly because companies are being shut out of the bond market to finance investments.
The Class C plan will give Zuckerberg more leeway in how he manages his fortune because he can more easily sell his stake in Meta for cash. It also would have helped him pay a proposed wealth tax on California billionaires that was recently rejected by 53% of voters in a referendum.
Meta's plan has prompted 10 shareholder lawsuits against Zuckerberg and other board members in Delaware Chancery Court for allegedly breaching their fiduciary duties by pushing through a deal the investors claim is unfair. Those cases have now been consolidated in one action.
"Public stockholders receive a pro rata stock dividend, but no corresponding governance protection or vote on the transaction," wrote attorneys for plaintiffs in one of the suits. "They also bear the economic and market costs of the new non-voting class and remain unable to influence most corporate decisions."
Meta earlier announced that board approval of the deal came after "the unanimous recommendation of a special committee of disinterested and independent directors" and that it was "in the best interests of Meta and its shareholders."
